units.unit: Researching Hong Kong's subdivided units and the rent control debate
Requests a source on the existing tenancy control ordinance and what it covers
Wants to show the current law caps increases within a tenancy but leaves initial rents unregulated
Wants to show the law excludes some kinds of SDU from key provisions
The sources cover ordinance scope, supply effects, enforcement, and legal risk
Wants to check the survey side
Has seen claims tenants would trade a rent rise for longer tenure or a faster housing offer
Has seen claims the real problem is queue length rather than price
Picks the trade-off first: tenants accepting a rent rise for longer tenure or a faster offer
Reached the position by working through the archive evidence rather than starting with it
SDU stock data looked stable at first
Separating second-generation controls (caps on increases) from first-generation ones (caps on levels) made the case for a hard cap on initial rents fall apart
Enforcement evidence and tenant survey pushed the same way
The paragraph 2 thesis is a conclusion from weighing those sources against each other
Point came from D6's elasticity estimate: a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes about 3–5 percent of stock over five years
D6's modelled Hong Kong scenario: a 15 percent cut leaves 3,000–4,000 households a year unable to enter
Berlin comparison in D7: caps protect incumbents but the bill is handed to those still outside
The idea that a hard cap shrinks the residual stock came from combining supply-elasticity data with the Berlin case
Point came from enforcement documents in the archive
D10p1 showed inspections cover under 6% of stock a year
D10p2: tenants least likely to complain—those without written agreements and newest arrivals—would be missed first
Combined those findings with Mrs Wong's situation in D4p1 (no written tenancy)
Concluded a hard cap would fail exactly the people it targets, forming the basis of paragraph 2
The 15–25 percent premium came from D1p1, read in the Room before drafting
Had noted it as background context on SDU pricing but didn't use it in earlier Room posts
The figure came from D2p2, read and cited in research notes but not discussed earlier in the Room
Brought it in because it shows rent burden got worse despite the 2021 ordinance, strengthening the argument that doing nothing isn't neutral
